Bayesian age-period-cohort model (bamp)

Source: R/model-apc_bayes.R
apc_bayes.Rd

Wrapper around the bamp package (Schmid and Held 2007): binomial likelihood for deaths given exposures, logit link, random walk priors of first or second order for age, period and cohort effects, optional overdispersion, MCMC with four chains. Forecasts extrapolate period and cohort effects as random walks for every posterior draw (bamp::predict_apc()), so the draws include parameter uncertainty.

Usage

apc_bayes(
  age = "rw2",
  period = "rw1",
  cohort = "rw1",
  overdispersion = FALSE,
  mcmc = mcmc_control(),
  resolution = c("observed", "grid"),
  shape_years = 5,
  max_refits = 1,
  coherent = FALSE,
  common_by = NULL,
  reference = NULL,
  cohort_deviation = FALSE,
  seed = NULL
)

Arguments

age, period, cohort

Prior for each effect: "rw1" or "rw2". The defaults use first-order random walks for period and cohort: with second-order random walks the extrapolated trends can make forecast intervals span orders of magnitude. First-order random walks carry the last period effect forward without a trend, so forecasts are biased when mortality keeps declining. The vignette "Bayesian age-period-cohort models with bamp" compares both.

overdispersion

Include cell-level overdispersion.

mcmc

MCMC settings from mcmc_control().

resolution

"observed" or "grid".

shape_years

Number of recent years used for the shape factors.

max_refits

Refits with longer chains if not converged.

coherent

Fit the strata of each group jointly with shared period and cohort effects and mean-reverting stratum deviations (see the section "Coherent model"); needs at least two strata per group.

common_by

Stratum variable(s) defining groups with their own common trend (coherent = TRUE), for example "sex" for the deprivation groups of each sex. NULL: one group of all strata.

reference

With coherent = TRUE: NULL (the deviations sum to zero over the strata of a group) or a named list of values of stratum variables that selects one reference stratum in every group, for example list(quintile = "England"), whose deviation is zero.

cohort_deviation

With coherent = TRUE: add AR(1) deviations of the strata along the cohorts.

seed

Seed of the native sampler (coherent = TRUE); NULL draws one from R's random number generator, so that set.seed() makes fits reproducible.

Value

A model specification.

Details

The wrapper makes bamp behave like every other model:

  • Resolution. With resolution = "observed" (default) the model is fitted where the deaths were observed: 5-year age groups with annual periods use periods_per_agegroup = 5 (Knorr-Held and Rainer 2001). Exposures are aggregated to the death cells. Age groups must have equal widths; an open last group is treated as one more group of that width.

  • Grid. Draws for age groups are mapped to the modelling grid with age-specific shape factors (single-year rate relative to its group rate, exposure-weighted to 1 within each group) estimated from the preprocessed training data of the last shape_years years. Use step_ungroup() in prep when deaths are grouped.

  • Convergence. bamp::checkConvergence() is called explicitly; a stratum that has not converged is refitted with twice as many iterations up to max_refits times, then reported as failed in the diagnostics.

  • Integers. bamp needs whole numbers; deaths and exposures are rounded and the largest relative rounding change is recorded.

Heterogeneity variants ("rw1+het", "rw2+het") are not offered because bamp::predict_apc() does not forecast them in bamp 3.0.0.

Coherent model (coherent = TRUE)

Fits the strata of each group of common_by (all strata without it) in one model, so that their forecasts do not diverge:

logit p[s, i, j] = mu + a[s] + theta[s, i] + phi[j] + psi[k] + d[s, j]

for stratum s, age group i, year j and cohort k, with binomial deaths given the exposures. The period effect phi and the cohort effect psi are shared and carry the common trend; their random-walk priors (orders period, cohort) are scaled to unit generalised variance (Sørbye and Rue 2014) and forecast as random walks. Each stratum has its own age effect theta[s, ] (random walk of order age, one precision for all strata) and level a[s]. The deviations d[s, ] of the strata from the shared period effect are stationary AR(1) series with a common coefficient rho (uniform prior on 0 to 1, sampled) and innovation precision; they sum to zero over the strata in every year, or, with reference, the deviation of the reference stratum is zero. Their forecasts revert towards zero, so the gaps between strata stay bounded. cohort_deviation = TRUE adds deviations c[s, k] of the same form along the cohorts. The precisions have Gamma priors with shape 1 and rates 0.5 (age) and 5e-4 (period, cohort, deviations). For the deviations the branch uses the rate 0.05, which dominates typical data: the posterior of their precision and the width of the forecast gaps are then set by the prior.

Sources. The model is the coherent model of the development branch "coherent_forecasting" of bamp (bamp_coherent(), by Chris Kypridemos), rewritten in this package because that branch is not released; when a bamp release contains it, apc_bayes(coherent = TRUE) will call bamp and the native sampler will be deprecated. Its published anchor is the two-population Bayesian APC model of Cairns et al. (2011): a common period trend and a mean-reverting AR(1) spread with level zero, population-specific age effects, a single-stage Bayesian fit, and two parameterisations, the spread between equal populations (their Section 4.5, the default here) and the spread from a dominant population (Section 4.4, reference). It differs from that paper, and these parts are package-specific (reference unknown): the binomial-logit likelihood and the random-walk smoothing priors of bamp (Schmid and Held 2007) in place of the Poisson likelihood with a random walk with drift and AR(2) cohort processes; one cohort effect shared by all strata (the alternative cohort hypothesis of their Section 4.3), with optional AR(1) cohort deviations in place of an AR(2) cohort spread; independent innovations of the common trend and the deviations (the paper: correlated); the priors; and more than two strata.

Sampler. Four chains of a Metropolis-Hastings sampler: all effects are proposed jointly from a Gaussian approximation of their conditional posterior (one Newton step from the current state, with sparse Cholesky factors; Rue and Held 2005, Section 4.4), the precisions are drawn from their Gamma conditionals, rho by a random-walk Metropolis step on the logit scale whose step size adapts during the burn-in only. Convergence is checked with the Gelman-Rubin statistic of the hyperparameters, the last period effect and the level of every stratum in the last year (rhat below 1.1); a group that has not converged is refitted with twice as many iterations up to max_refits times. Overdispersion is not available in the coherent model.

Draws are posterior draws of the rates. Predictive draws (mt_forecast(predictive = TRUE)) add Poisson variation of the deaths given the rates of each draw and the exposures, as for the other models of expected rates; no other observation noise is added. bamp's binomial likelihood and its overdispersion term (overdispersion = TRUE) are not carried into the predictive draws: the overdispersion only enters the posterior of the rates. If intervals are too narrow on real data, that is a property of the model (see recalibrated(), ensemble(), or overdispersed models such as stanmomo(family = "nb")).

References

Knorr-Held L, Rainer E (2001). Prognosis of lung cancer mortality in West Germany: a case study in Bayesian prediction. Biostatistics 2(1): 109-129.

Schmid VJ, Held L (2007). Bayesian age-period-cohort modeling and prediction: BAMP. Journal of Statistical Software 21(8): 1-15. doi:10.18637/jss.v021.i08

Cairns AJG, Blake D, Dowd K, Coughlan GD, Khalaf-Allah M (2011). Bayesian stochastic mortality modelling for two populations. ASTIN Bulletin 41(1): 29-59. doi:10.2143/AST.41.1.2084385

Gelman A, Rubin DB (1992). Inference from iterative simulation using multiple sequences. Statistical Science 7(4): 457-472. doi:10.1214/ss/1177011136

Rue H, Held L (2005). Gaussian Markov Random Fields: Theory and Applications. Chapman and Hall/CRC, Boca Raton.

Sørbye SH, Rue H (2014). Scaling intrinsic Gaussian Markov random field priors in spatial modelling. Spatial Statistics 8: 39-51. doi:10.1016/j.spasta.2013.06.004

Examples

# \donttest{
if (requireNamespace("bamp", quietly = TRUE)) {
  x <- mt_example(years = 2005:2019)
  fit <- mt_fit(apc_bayes(mcmc = mcmc_control("test")), x, prep = mt_prep(step_ungroup()))
  fc <- mt_forecast(fit, h = 5, n_draws = 200, seed = 1)
}
# }
# coherent model of the two sexes (native sampler, no bamp needed)
# \donttest{
x <- mt_example(years = 2005:2019)
fit <- mt_fit(apc_bayes(coherent = TRUE, mcmc = mcmc_control("test"), seed = 1), x,
              prep = mt_prep(step_ungroup()))
# }
